items.title: 14.1.3 Fundamental Mathematical Operations for Vectors in Space

blocks.title: Numbering note
blocks.text: The textbook prints this heading as 14.1.4 (Book# 14.1.4). The book has no 14.1.1, so the portal numbers the sub-headings of 14.1 in sequence as 14.1.1 to 14.1.8; 14.1.3 here is the book's 14.1.4.
We define addition and scalar multiplication in \(R^{3}\) by:
(i) Addition of vectors: For any two vectors \(\underline{u} = [x, y, z]\) and \(\underline{v} = [x', y', z']\) we have

blocks.latex: \underline{u} + \underline{v} = [x, y, z] + [x', y', z'] \\ = [x + x',\ y + y',\ z + z']
blocks.text_alt: u plus v equals x plus x prime, y plus y prime, z plus z prime

blocks.text: (ii) Scalar Multiplication of a vector: For \(\underline{u} = [x, y, z]\) and \(a \in R\), we have

blocks.latex: a\underline{u} = a[x, y, z] = [ax, ay, az]
blocks.text_alt: a u equals a x, a y, a z

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Exactly as in the plane, but with a third component. Example: \(\underline{u} = [1, 2, 3]\), \(\underline{v} = [4, -1, 0]\).
\(\underline{u} + \underline{v} = [1 + 4,\ 2 + (-1),\ 3 + 0] = [5, 1, 3]\)
\(2\underline{u} = [2, 4, 6]\)
The dash in \(x'\) (read \"x dash\") is only a label telling us it is the x-component of the second vector; it is not a derivative.

The set of all ordered triples \([x, y, z]\) of real numbers, together with the rules of addition and scalar multiplication is called the set of vectors in \(R^{3}\). For the vector \(\underline{u} = [x, y, z]\), \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) are called the components of \(\underline{u}\). The definition of vectors in \(R^{3}\) states that vector addition and scalar multiplication are to be carried out also for vectors in space just as for vectors in the plane. Similarly we define in \(R^{3}\):
(a) The negative of the vector \(\underline{u} = [x, y, z]\) as

blocks.text_alt: minus u equals minus one times u equals minus x, minus y, minus z

blocks.text: (b) The difference of two vectors \(\underline{v} = [x', y', z']\) and \(\underline{w} = [x'', y'', z'']\) as

blocks.text_alt: v minus w equals v plus minus w equals x prime minus x double prime, and so on

blocks.text: (d) Equality of two vectors: Tow vectors \(\underline{v} = [x', y', z']\) and \(\underline{w} = [x'', y'', z'']\) are equal, that is \(\underline{v} = \underline{w}\), if and only if \(x' = x''\), \(y' = y''\) and \(z' = z''\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "Tow vectors"; it should read "Two vectors".

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
With \(\underline{v} = [3, 0, 5]\) and \(\underline{w} = [1, 2, 3]\):
\(-\underline{w} = [-1, -2, -3]\)
\(\underline{v} - \underline{w} = [3 - 1,\ 0 - 2,\ 5 - 3] = [2, -2, 2]\)
\(\underline{v} + \underline{0} = \underline{v}\), and \(\underline{w} + (-\underline{w}) = \underline{0}\).
Equality gives three ordinary equations at once: \([a, 2, b + 1] = [3, 2, 5]\) means \(a = 3\) and \(b + 1 = 5\), so \(b = 4\).

For any point \(P(x, y, z)\) in \(R^{3}\), a vector \(\underline{u} = [x, y, z]\) is represented by a directed line segment \(\underline{OP}\), whose initial point is at origin. Such vectors are called position vectors in \(R^{3}\).
If \(A(x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1})\) and \(B(x'', y'', z'')\) are two points then position vector \(\underline{AB}\) is \(\underline{AB} = \underline{v} = [x' - x'',\ y' - y'',\ z' - z'']\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The book's formula does not match its own points: it names \(A(x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1})\) and \(B(x'', y'', z'')\) but then subtracts \(x''\) from \(x'\), which belong to neither point. The vector from \(A\) to \(B\) is \"terminal point minus initial point\":
\[\underline{AB} = \underline{OB} - \underline{OA}\]
\[= [x'' - x_{1},\ y'' - y_{1},\ z'' - z_{1}]\]
With the usual names \(A(x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1})\), \(B(x_{2}, y_{2}, z_{2})\): \(\underline{AB} = [x_{2} - x_{1},\ y_{2} - y_{1},\ z_{2} - z_{1}]\). (The same result appears correctly in 14.1.7.)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why \"terminal minus initial\"? Going from \(O\) to \(A\) and then from \(A\) to \(B\) is the same as going straight from \(O\) to \(B\): \(\underline{OA} + \underline{AB} = \underline{OB}\). So \(\underline{AB} = \underline{OB} - \underline{OA}\).
Example: \(A(1, 2, 3)\), \(B(4, 0, 5)\): \(\underline{AB} = [4 - 1,\ 0 - 2,\ 5 - 3] = [3, -2, 2]\), and \(\underline{BA} = [-3, 2, -2]\).
Strictly, \(\underline{AB}\) is not itself a position vector (it does not start at \(O\)); it is found from the position vectors of \(A\) and \(B\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Add, subtract and multiply by a scalar component by component.
\(-\underline{u} = [-x, -y, -z]\); \(\underline{0} = [0, 0, 0]\).
Two vectors are equal exactly when all three components are equal.
Position vector of \(P\): \(\underline{OP} = [x, y, z]\).
\(\underline{AB} = \underline{OB} - \underline{OA}\): terminal minus initial.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Subtracting in the wrong order: \(\underline{AB}\) is \(B - A\), not \(A - B\).
Forgetting to change every sign in \(-\underline{w}\): \(-[1, -2, 3] = [-1, 2, -3]\).
Multiplying only the first component by the scalar: \(2[1, 2, 3] = [2, 4, 6]\), not \([2, 2, 3]\).
